about.title: Chula Vista Product Liability Claims
about.longDescription:
A defective product rarely announces itself. It might be a space heater that overheats in a Chula Vista apartment, a child's car seat that fails on the way down Olympic Parkway, a pressure cooker lid that gives way, or a power tool that jumps out of your hands on a job site near Main Street. More than 265,000 people live in this corner of San Diego County, and each of them relies every day on products they never designed and cannot take apart to inspect.

California law recognizes that imbalance. Under strict liability, you generally do not need to prove the maker was careless. What matters is whether the product was defective — in its design, in how it was built, or in how its risks were explained — and whether that defect caused your injury. Responsibility can reach the manufacturer, the distributor, and the store that sold it.

LawProactive is a free service, not a law firm. We connect Chula Vista residents with an independent product liability attorney who works on contingency. Keep the product, its packaging, and your receipts.

items.title: Every Link in the Chain
items.desc: Manufacturers, distributors, and retailers can each be held responsible under California law. An independent attorney can identify all of them, including a local Chula Vista seller and an out-of-state maker.

items.question: I bought the product at a store on Broadway in Chula Vista, but it was made overseas. Who can actually be held responsible?
items.answer: California's strict liability rules extend to everyone in the chain of distribution, not just the factory that built the item. That means the retailer here in Chula Vista, any distributor in between, and the manufacturer may all be responsible. An attorney can sort out which parties are reachable and how the claim should be directed.

items.question: Do I have to prove the company was negligent to have a product liability claim?
items.answer: Usually not. In California, a product liability claim generally runs on strict liability, so you typically need to show the product had a design, manufacturing, or warning defect and that the defect caused your injury. Whether the maker was careless is often beside the point. An attorney can explain how this applies to your specific product.

items.question: I threw the broken product away after I got hurt. Is my claim over?
items.answer: Not necessarily, though the product itself is often the strongest evidence, so losing it makes things harder. Photos, receipts, packaging, the same model purchased separately, medical records, and witness accounts may still help establish what went wrong. Reach out as soon as you can so an attorney can assess what remains and advise you on next steps.
